title: Politics live: Marles apologises to LGBTQ+ veterans; Australia and Solomon Islands sign ‘historic’ treaty
description:
• Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Wells says AI investment and creative protections not a ‘zero-sum game’

Weighing into the gigantic debate that is AI companies wanting to scrape Australian data to train models versus creatives who want to protect their work, Anika Wells says it’s not a ‘zero-sum’ game.

I reject this sort of zero-sum game where building Australian sovereignty in AI must come at the expense of creatives or at diminishing the rights of creatives. At the moment, yes, we want deals, but we want creatives paid properly for their work. And the situation that we find ourselves in at the moment is that they’re not. They have no control and often no payment for their work.
text: National apology to LBGTQ+ veterans a ‘milestone’
GLBTI Rights in Ageing Inc. (GRAI) has welcomed the deputy prime minister and defence minister’s apology to LGBTQ+ veterans this morning, calling it a milestone after years of campaigning.
GRAI chair, David Gibson, who was discharged from the Australian army due to his bisexuality, was in the House for the apology.
In a statement he said:

double quotation markFor many veterans, the apology marks a milestone after years of pressing for recognition, sharing their experiences with the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, and giving evidence to the Senate inquiry. The legislative reforms that followed offer Australia a way to recognise both their service and the harm they experienced.
‘Unwelcome but unsurprising’: Chalmers responds to inflation data
Treasurer Jim Chalmers - who will probably face some more hostile questioning from the opposition today in QT – says the latest inflation data ticking up from 4.3% to 4.9% was widely anticipated.
He said global oil prices was the biggest influence on the monthly figures, with automotive fuel prices rising 6.3% in October.
In the government’s defence, Chalmers says “every major advanced economy has had a rate rise” since September.

double quotation markThis is another unwelcome but unsurprising reminder of the pressure Australians are under. We had an inflation challenge in our economy before the conflict in the Middle East but the war is making it worse. This inflation challenge is the primary influence on the budget update we will finalise in the coming weeks and release in December.
Victorian Labor proposes new AI workplace rules
With just a handful of days until polling day, Victorian Labor has made a handful of announcements around AI and the workplace.

Labor promises to force employers to disclose when they’re using AI in the recruitment process and to give applicants the right to know if an automated decision was made. They’re also requiring the use of AI in recruitment to be tested for discrimination and they will make companies legally responsible if discrimination occurs because of AI.

There are also announcements for gig workers. This follows the death of HungryPanda delivery driver Feng Jianming in Melbourne’s CBD. They said they will work with WorkSafe to look into making the following changes:
Giving WorkSafe to audit potentially dangerous algorithims that reward dangerous speed.
Covering riders when they are hurt on the job, and stopping the platforms from fining riders for refusing dangerous deliveries.
In the statement, the premier, Ben Carroll, said: “Platforms must be on the hook for managing safety risks, too – they share a responsibility.”
Coalition, Greens and crossbench rally against government over home births access

The independent senator David Pocock, the opposition, the Greens and other crossbenchers have come together to put pressure on the government over an impending rule change that could be detrimental for women accessing home births in Australia.
This takes a bit of explaining so bear with me here – it’s important.
From 1 January a longstanding professional indemnity insurance exemption for privately practising midwives attending home births will expire.

In Australia, a planned home birth legally requires two midwives – the first midwife must be endorsed but the supporting second midwife does not have to be. Just 5% of midwives in Australia are endorsed.
The concern is this will mean women – particularly in rural and regional areas – will lose access to a home birth.

Pocock has put forward a motion (which he has the numbers for) to call on the government to extend the indemnity insurance exemption for two years, and work with women, midwives and the sector to come up with a better solution. He has told the Senate:

double quotation markIn just over five weeks, the ability for Australian women to choose to give birth at home will be severely compromised. While the government has supported the development of a new insurance product, we’re hearing overwhelmingly from midwives across the country that it is not fit for purpose. The insurance is prohibitively expensive for many second attending midwives and requires them to be endorsed, despite the primary already being endorsed.
Inflation jumps to 4.9%
Surging fuel costs have helped drive inflation to 4.9% in the year to October, from 4.3%, as cost-of-living pressures peak in the lead-up to Christmas.

The latest figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics come two days after Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, stood up in parliament to warn Australians that economic conditions would get worse before they got better.
The Reserve Bank’s preferred gauge of underlying price pressures, the trimmed mean measure of inflation, lifted to 3.8%, from 3.6% in the month before.
Economists are hopeful that inflation will ease through 2027 to be back below 3% in a year’s time.
And amid fears of a more severe economic downturn, financial markets before the release of the latest data were pricing in an RBA rate cut by August.
Deputy prime minister apologises to LGBTQ+ veterans

There has been a lot going on in parliament today, while the Australian and Solomon Islands prime ministers were holding a press conference, the deputy PM and defence minister, Richard Marles, was giving a long overdue national apology to LGBTQ+ veterans.
Until as late as 1990, the ADF maintained a policy prohibiting homosexual members from serving, resulting in discharges and convictions because of consensual same‑sex activity.

A parliamentary committee in July recommended the government issue a national apology to LGBTQ+ veterans and service personnel who experienced discrimination at the hands of the Australian defence force.
Marles told the House:

double quotation markIt is a shameful chapter in the history of the Australian defence force. And it is one that we must confront with honesty … Lifting the [homosexuality] ban could not hand back careers. Careers that in some cases, had barely begun, or some that had been decades in the making the [homosexuality] ban could not hand back incomes … or even the right to call themselves a veteran at all. Some never told their families why they came home early. Some have never marched on Anzac Day. To you I say: you and your families offered this nation everything that service asks. In return our nation offered condemnation, derision, and suspicion. This country did not keep faith with you. But today it says sorry.
What’s in the Solomon Islands treaty?
The Solomon Islands will not allow its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base under a landmark treaty sealed with Australia.
Under the agreement, Honiara has committed that its sensitive infrastructure shall remain “free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access”.
This is a major win for Australia, which has been working to stop China from gaining a military foothold in the region.
Canberra was alarmed when Solomon Islands and Beijing signed a controversial security pact in 2022.
Solomon Islanders will also have improved visa arrangements, being able to stay in Australia for longer periods. New opportunities in Australia’s early childhood and aged care sectors will open.
Building on the Albanese government’s successful sport diplomacy, this treaty includes a sweetener for an “expanded soccer partnership” to develop and deepen opportunities for local talent.
Labor used the planned new NRL team based in Papua New Guinea to seal its alliance with Port Moresby.
‘Massive win’: Monique Ryan celebrates private health insurance backdown
The crossbencher and medical doctor Monique Ryan has celebrated the government’s backdown to carve out pensioners from its private health insurance legislation.
It means people over 65 – who are not pensioners – will lose their additional private health insurance rebates, putting them on par with everyone else.
Ryan said her commissioned analysis of the policy by the Parliamentary Budget Office showed it was “a cash grab from pensioners”:

double quotation markFantastic to secure a massive win for older Australians today! From the moment this measure was announced in April, I’ve been fighting to secure affordable private health insurance for older Australians. It’s been wonderful to work across the Parliament to successfully oppose a poorly conceived, unfair and unreasonable bill.
‘I welcome the motion of no confidence’: Solomon Islands PM Matthew Wale
Matthew Wale says he would welcome a motion of no confidence, and that the decision to sign today’s treaty was taken with his entire caucus and cabinet.
Wale faced a no confidence motion in September, before the Pacific Islands Forum, which was then withdrawn.
Wale is unfazed when asked if he could withstand any future challenges:

double quotation markSo far as my leadership is concerned, the decision to sign this treaty is a decision taken by my caucus and my entire cabinet, there was unity to sign and that is what we have done. I welcome the motion of no confidence and I look forward to it.
Matthew Wale can’t comment on end of the China pact
Why? Because he says there was a non-disclosure agreement attached to it.
Wale ordered a review of the pact with Beijing signed in April 2022, under his predecessor, Manasseh Sogavare.
Wale’s decision reverses Sogavare’s alignment with Beijing, in favour of Australia.
Wale is asked what the reaction from China has been that the pact, which expires in April 2027, will not be renewed. He also won’t say.

double quotation markUnfortunately there is a nondisclosure clause in the treaty with China, security pact, and the police an agreement so I am unable to talk about that. We have ongoing discussions with China.
